Kena Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
Like the Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad, the first in the series of the ten उपनिषद्स् considered ancient and more important, the Kena Upaniṣad (which is the second) also derives its name from the very first word, ‘kena’ (‘by whom’) with which it begins. Since it belongs to the Talavakāra Brāhmaṇa of the Sāmaveda, it is also known as the Talavakāra Upaniṣad. The तलवकारस् were those who could sing the Sāmans with ताल or keeping time with regular beats of hand. (This seems to have gone out of practice in later years.)
It has four khaṇḍas or sections, the first two being in poetry and the last two in prose. The total number of verses is 35.
The Upaniṣad opens with a question, perhaps by an inquiring disciple, whether there is any entity behind the sense-organs like the ear or the organ of speech or even the मिन्द्, that impels them to work. The teacher replies that there is, and that he is the eye of the eye, the ear of the ear, the speech of the speech and the मिन्द् of the मिन्द्. They are able to function because of his presence and power. They do not know him whereas he knows them all. He is ब्रह्मन्. It is almost impossible to impart the knowledge concerning him to others since his characteristics are beyond the comprehension of the senses and the मिन्द्.
Since ब्रह्मन् (as the आत्मन् in us, our very Self) is the real knower of all that is known through the senses and the मिन्द् and itself is not an object of knowledge, one can never say that one has known him nor not known him. Awareness of ब्रह्मन् is felt at every moment of our life. It is only the direct experience of this आत्मन् that gives us real strength and इम्मोर्तलित्य्. If one misses the grand opportunity given through this human birth for getting that experience and इम्मोर्तलित्य् through it, it is a terrible loss. This is the gist of the teaching of the second section.
The third section teaches through an interesting story that ब्रह्मन् is supreme and that even the gods in हेअवेन्, like इन्द्र and अग्नि, could win their battles against the असुरस् or demons only because of the power imparted to them by him. They were made to learn this bitter lesson after being humiliated by ब्रह्मन् disguised as a यक्ष, a demigod, far inferior to them!
The fourth section is a continuation of the teaching of the third. It is the goddess Umā हैमवती that is teaching इन्द्र, the king of the gods. ब्रह्मन् who appeared before इन्द्र just for a moment like lightning is also the आत्मन्, the Self in every one of us. One has to meditate upon him as ‘tadvana,’ ‘the one who is highly desirable’. This is understandable since ‘he’ is really ‘me’. One who realises him will therefore be liked by all beings.
The Upaniṣad ends with the declaration that तपस् (austerity), दम (self-control) and कर्म (works and duties ordained by the scriptures) are the means of attaining ब्रह्मन्. So also a study of the वेदस् and their subsidiary sciences and सत्य or truth.
And, one who realises ब्रह्मन् by these means, gets rid of his sins and is established in ‘svargaloka’ (the world of ब्रह्मन्).
See also ĪŚĀVĀSYA UPANIṢAD and UPANIṢADS.
